_design_note: Replaces the fine-tuned Flan-T5 recommender, which was trained on 7 examples
for 100 optimizer steps and ended at loss 3.2368 -- it never learned them, so
a hardcoded dictionary supplied the text in practice anyway. A table is
strictly better here: exact, reviewable, versioned, and incapable of
hallucinating a chemical or a dose.
SAFETY MODEL. Every chemical entry carries a `status`:
reviewed            -- dose/PHI checked against the cited source on `checked_on`
needs_verification  -- active ingredient noted, dose deliberately null
treatments.py will NOT emit a dose, PHI or application rate for anything that
is not `reviewed`. Unverified entries surface the active-ingredient name and a
pointer to CIBRC, never a number. Cultural practices carry no dose and are
Every chemical entry here is currently `needs_verification`: the CIBRC
crop-wise tables are PDFs that were not machine-read when this file was
written, and inventing a dose for an agrochemical is exactly the harm this
table exists to prevent. Populating them is a data-entry task against the
cited PDFs, not a code task.

sources.name: CIBRC — Major Uses of Pesticides (crop-wise / pest-wise)
sources.authority: Central Insecticides Board & Registration Committee, Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine & Storage, Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, Government of India
sources.note: The authoritative register of what is legally usable on which crop in India. Refreshed quarterly. A product with no potato label claim must not be recommended for potato.

sources.name: CIBRC — Banned / restricted / refused registration
sources.note: Must be cross-checked before any entry is promoted to `reviewed`. Several actives commonly cited in older literature are now restricted.

sources.name: ICAR–Central Potato Research Institute, Shimla
sources.note: Package of practices and the INDO-BLIGHTCAST late-blight forecasting model.

global_disclaimer: Guidance only, not a prescription. Confirm the product, dose, pre-harvest interval and legality for your crop and district with a licensed agronomist or your State Agricultural University extension officer before applying anything. Always read the product label — the label is the law.

Healthy.summary: No visible symptoms of the seven tracked conditions. This is not a clean bill of health for the field — it is one leaf at one moment.
cultural: Keep scouting. Walk the field twice weekly, and after every rain, looking at lower and inner leaves where infection starts.
Maintain spacing and remove weeds so the canopy dries quickly after rain or irrigation.
Irrigate at soil level. Wet foliage is the single biggest driver of foliar disease.
Remove and destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles — they carry inoculum between seasons.
Use certified seed and rotate away from solanaceous crops (potato, tomato, brinjal, chilli) for 3–4 years.
Record what you planted, when, and what you applied. Records are what make next season's decisions better than guesses.
do_not: Do not spray a fungicide or insecticide because a scan came back healthy. Prophylactic spraying on a symptom-free crop wastes money, accelerates resistance, and harms beneficial insects.
Healthy.escalate_if: Symptoms appear on more than a few plants, spread visibly between scouting visits, or you cannot identify what you are seeing.

Phytophthora.severity: very high — can destroy a crop in under two weeks under cool, wet conditions
Phytophthora.summary: Water-soaked lesions with a pale halo, often starting at leaf tips and margins, with white sporulation on the underside in humid weather. Spreads explosively when nights are cool and humidity is high.
cultural: Destroy cull piles and volunteer plants before the season starts — they are the primary inoculum source.
Plant certified, disease-free seed tubers; avoid seed from an affected field.
Improve drainage and avoid overhead irrigation. Raised beds help in heavy soils.
Increase row spacing to speed canopy drying.
Destroy the haulm before harvest so tubers are not exposed to spores washing down.
Do not harvest in wet conditions; cure tubers dry before storage.

ppe: respirator where the label requires one
chemical.resistance_note: Multi-site protectant, low resistance risk. Use as the partner in a mix rather than relying on single-site actives alone.

chemical.role: curative, only once infection is present
chemical.resistance_note: IMPORTANT: metalaxyl resistance in P. infestans is established in India. Do not use metalaxyl as a solo curative and do not repeat it in consecutive sprays. Alternate modes of action, and confirm local resistance status with your State Agricultural University before relying on it.

chemical.role: curative alternative where metalaxyl resistance is suspected
chemical.resistance_note: Rotate modes of action across the season. Never apply the same single-site active twice in succession.

Phytophthora.forecasting: This is the disease where prediction beats reaction. INDO-BLIGHTCAST (ICAR-CPRI Shimla) forecasts late-blight risk from temperature and relative humidity for the Indo-Gangetic plains. A weather-driven warning is worth more than any post-hoc diagnosis.
Phytophthora.escalate_if: Lesions are spreading between scouting visits, or weather is forecast cool and wet. Late blight moves faster than an advice cycle — contact an extension officer the same day.

Fungi.common_name: Fungal leaf disease (early blight and similar)
Fungi.pathogen: commonly Alternaria solani; this class covers several foliar fungi
Fungi.summary: Dark lesions with concentric rings, often on older lower leaves first, on a yellowing background. Favoured by warm weather with alternating wet and dry spells.
cultural: Remove and destroy infected plant debris; do not leave haulm in the field.
Rotate away from solanaceous crops for at least 2–3 years.
Irrigate at soil level and avoid prolonged leaf wetness.
Maintain balanced nitrogen — deficient plants are markedly more susceptible.
Choose less susceptible varieties where available for your region.
Space rows for airflow so the canopy dries quickly.

ppe: respirator where the label requires one
chemical.resistance_note: Multi-site. NOTE: restricted or withdrawn in some jurisdictions (including the EU) — confirm current Indian registration and any residue limits for your export market before use.
Single-site, HIGH resistance risk. Limit applications per season as the label specifies, always alternate with a multi-site partner, and never use it curatively on its own.

Fungi.escalate_if: More than roughly 5% of leaf area is affected across the field, or lesions reach the upper canopy.

Bacteria.common_name: Bacterial disease (blackleg / soft rot / bacterial wilt)
Bacteria.pathogen: commonly Pectobacterium / Dickeya spp., or Ralstonia solanacearum
Bacteria.severity: high — and largely not curable in-season
Bacteria.summary: Dark, water-soaked, often slimy or foul-smelling lesions; wilting that does not recover overnight; blackened stem bases. Spread by water, tools, insects and infected seed.
cultural: There is no effective chemical cure for bacterial disease in the field. Management is sanitation and exclusion.
Remove and destroy affected plants immediately, including tubers — do not compost them.
Disinfect knives, tools and boots between plants and between plots.
Use certified disease-free seed. Avoid cutting seed tubers where you can; if you must, disinfect between cuts.
Improve drainage and avoid overhead irrigation. Never irrigate from a source downstream of an affected field.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 3–4 years; Ralstonia in particular persists in soil.
Do not handle plants when foliage is wet.

chemical.active_ingredient: copper-based bactericide (e.g. copper oxychloride / copper hydroxide)
chemical.role: suppressive only — reduces surface spread, does not cure infected plants
chemical.resistance_note: Copper tolerance occurs in some bacterial populations. Repeated copper also accumulates in soil. Treat as an adjunct to sanitation, never a substitute.

do_not: Do not expect a spray to rescue a bacterial infection. Removing infected material and disinfecting tools does more than any product.
Bacteria.escalate_if: Always. Bacterial wilt in particular is a notifiable concern in some states and affects what you can plant next season — involve an extension officer.

Virus.pathogen: Potato virus Y, Potato leafroll virus and others
Virus.severity: high — cumulative across seasons through infected seed
Virus.summary: Mosaic mottling, crinkling, leaf rolling, stunting, vein clearing. Symptoms are often mistaken for nutrient deficiency or herbicide damage.
cultural: There is no cure. A virus-infected plant stays infected — management is removing sources and controlling vectors.
Rogue out symptomatic plants early, including tubers, and destroy them.
Use certified virus-tested seed. This is the single most effective control by a wide margin.
Control aphid vectors, which spread PVY and PLRV, and manage weed hosts along field margins.
Do not save seed from a field showing virus symptoms — infection compounds season on season.
Disinfect tools; PVY in particular transmits mechanically on blades.
Plant resistant varieties where available for your region.

chemical.active_ingredient: insecticide targeting aphid vectors (active depends on local resistance)
chemical.role: vector suppression only — has no effect on the virus itself
ppe: respirator where the label requires one
chemical.resistance_note: Aphid insecticide resistance is widespread and local. Ask your State Agricultural University which actives still work in your district. Rotate modes of action. Note that killing aphids does not stop non-persistent transmission of PVY, which happens within seconds of probing — seed health matters far more.

Virus.escalate_if: More than a few plants are affected, or you intend to save seed from this field — get the crop tested first.

Pest.pathogen: not a pathogen — chewing or sucking arthropod damage
Pest.severity: variable — depends entirely on which pest and at what growth stage
Pest.summary: Holes, notching, skeletonised tissue, mines, stippling or curling. Damage type identifies the culprit, and the culprit determines the response.
cultural: Identify the pest before treating. 'Pest' is not an actionable diagnosis — an aphid, a tuber moth and a mite need three different responses.
Practise IPM: scout and use thresholds, protect natural enemies, and treat only when damage justifies it.
Use pheromone traps for potato tuber moth to time any intervention.
Earth up well so tubers are not exposed to tuber moth.
Encourage beneficials — ladybirds, lacewings and parasitoid wasps — by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.
Row covers help during vulnerable early growth.
Remove and destroy heavily infested plant parts.

chemical.role: soft-bodied pests: aphids, mites, whitefly, early instars
chemical.resistance_note: Lower impact on beneficials than broad-spectrum insecticides. Contact action — coverage matters, including leaf undersides.

chemical.active_ingredient: selective insecticide matched to the identified pest
chemical.role: only after the pest is identified and a threshold is exceeded
ppe: respirator where the label requires one
chemical.resistance_note: Choose the narrowest-spectrum option that works. Rotate modes of action across the season. Broad-spectrum sprays commonly trigger secondary mite and aphid outbreaks by removing predators.

do_not: Do not spray a broad-spectrum insecticide on an unidentified pest. It often makes the problem worse by killing the predators that were holding it down.
Pest.escalate_if: You cannot identify the pest, or damage continues after an intervention.

Nematode.pathogen: Globodera spp., Meloidogyne spp., Pratylenchus spp.
Nematode.severity: high and persistent — soil-borne, and it builds up over seasons
Nematode.summary: Patchy stunting, yellowing and wilting in the heat that recovers overnight, with galls or cysts on roots. Above-ground symptoms are easily mistaken for drought or nutrient stress, so diagnosis needs a soil or root test.
cultural: Confirm with a soil test before acting. Nematode management is expensive and multi-season, so it is worth knowing the species and population first.
Rotate with non-host crops — cereals such as maize or wheat — for several seasons.
Plant resistant varieties where available; for potato cyst nematode this is the mainstay.
Use certified seed and clean equipment. Nematodes travel in soil on machinery and boots.
Add organic matter to support the soil's natural antagonists.
Solarise soil before planting where the climate allows.
Consider a trap or biofumigant crop (e.g. mustard) in the rotation.
Control volunteer potatoes, which let the population persist through a rotation.

chemical.active_ingredient: registered nematicide, or a bio-nematicide such as Purpureocillium lilacinum
chemical.role: population suppression alongside rotation, not a standalone fix
ppe: respirator — several conventional nematicides are highly toxic
chemical.resistance_note: Conventional nematicides are among the most acutely toxic agrochemicals in use and several are restricted or banned. Do not select one without professional advice. Verify current registration and restriction status before considering any product.

do_not: Do not apply a nematicide on a visual diagnosis alone. Confirm with a soil test first.
Nematode.escalate_if: Always. Nematode management is a multi-season rotation decision, not a spray decision — involve an extension officer or your State Agricultural University.
